lines.text: I've talked myself around half the room, which isn't helpful, so here's the useful part: I suspect {target}.
I suspect {target}. Before I wander into another theory, I'd like us to hear their answer.
I don't trust {target} yet. Can we question them before I bury the point in another explanation?
I'm accusing {target}. I'll stop there long enough for them to answer.
My suspicion keeps returning to {target}. I want the room to consider them as a suspect.
{target}, I have questions about your position, quite a lot actually, but let's start with whether we should trust you.
I could introduce this more gently, or at greater length, so I'll spare us one of those and accuse {target}.
My suspicion is pointed at {target}; the rest of this sentence is just me trying to make that less uncomfortable.
Let's put {target} under scrutiny before I get distracted by the wording of scrutiny, which I can already feel happening.
I have too many possibilities in my head, but my accusation right now is against {target}.
{target}, I'm not announcing a whole grand theory here, just saying that I don't trust you enough to move on.
I suspect {target}. That's the point I meant to reach before this sentence got away from me.
I deny the accusation against me. I have more to say, naturally, but that's the important part.
You've accused the wrong person. Please hear my answer before deciding what you think it means.
I'm defending myself here: my habit of talking too much doesn't prove your accusation.
I dispute the case against me. An explanation isn't a confession, even when it takes me a while.
I deny it. Let me answer your questions one at a time so we can actually get somewhere.
I disagree with the accusation against me. Please judge the case rather than the length of my answer.
Don't condemn me on suspicion alone. I want you to hear my side before reaching that decision.
I'm nervous and talking too much, but I'm still saying the accusation against me is wrong.
My long answer doesn't make me guilty. I reject the accusation, however many words that takes.
I don't accept your conclusion about me. Give me a fair hearing and I'll try to stay on the point.
I dispute the accusation. Ask me one question and let me finish the answer before the next one.
Please don't vote against me yet. I deny the charge, and I want that heard clearly.
I should probably stop circling the introduction and give you the important bit, which is that I'm the {role}.
My role is {role}, and yes, I did have a longer announcement prepared, but this seems like the wrong moment for it.
Let me put something definite on the record before the conversation escapes again: I'm claiming {role}.
I was waiting for a neat opening, there wasn't one, anyway, I'm the {role}.
You need to know my role rather than my thoughts about when to reveal it, so here it is: {role}.
This is the part of my explanation you should keep if you forget the rest: I'm the {role}.
I've made the lead-in much longer than the information itself, which is simply that my role is {role}.
For everyone who understandably lost track of where I was going, I am declaring myself the {role}.
I could keep you waiting while I explain my timing, but let's do the useful thing first: I'm the {role}.
My public claim, with the surrounding commentary removed as much as I can manage, is {role}.
I agree with {target}, and I was going to explain my agreement in detail, but agreement seems a good place to stop.
I agree with {target}'s point. They've said what I was trying to express, in fewer words.
Can we keep {target}'s point in the conversation? I'm supporting it, despite having taken a scenic route to say so.
Yes to {target}, specifically to that argument, before my general enthusiasm makes my position sound larger than it is.
I'm on {target}'s side of this question, which is perhaps the shortest version of what I wanted to contribute.
What {target} said makes sense to me, and I don't want that buried under all the other things I also want to say.
I was halfway into my own explanation when {target}'s point landed, so I'm abandoning mine and agreeing with theirs.
I'm supporting the point {target} just made. Please don't let the rest of my sentence obscure that.
I'd like to underline {target}'s point because I agree with it. Verbally, since we aren't handing around pens.
{target}, you've persuaded me on that part; I could keep speaking, but it wouldn't make the yes any clearer.
I disagree with {target}, and the difficult part is explaining the disagreement without accidentally giving you my entire train of thought.
{target}, I see where you're going, or I think I do, but I don't want us arriving at that conclusion.
Can we pause on the point from {target}? I'm not convinced, even though I have used rather a lot of time considering it.
I can't support {target}'s argument, and I wanted to say that before my attempt to be polite became mistaken for agreement.
There's a difference between hearing {target} out and accepting the conclusion, and I'm very much doing the first one here.
My answer to {target} is no, with several qualifications I could talk through if we actually need them.
I keep trying to follow {target}'s reasoning to the same place, but somehow I arrive at disagreement every time.
{target}, I'm going to challenge that view, not introduce three unrelated subjects, though I appreciate how unlikely that may sound.
I don't share the position {target} has taken, which is the important part of this unusually well-signposted contribution.
We should hear another view besides {target}'s, and mine starts with not accepting the point they just made.
I had all these small things I thought I'd say to them later, and now later is a word that doesn't work.
The room sounds different with someone missing, which I know is obvious, but it's the only thing I can keep talking around.
I'd normally fill a silence like this, then apologize for filling it, but a death leaves a rather different kind of silence.
Can we acknowledge the person behind the report before we turn the report into the next topic of discussion?
I'm trying to talk about the death rather than around it, and discovering I don't know where to begin.
There's one fewer person to interrupt my stories, and that's a miserable way to realize how much a voice mattered.
I was about to say we'll discuss this when everyone gets here, which shows how slowly my mouth has caught up.
We should remember that someone died, even while we do the necessary business of asking what it means for everyone left.
I keep wanting another detail to make the report feel less final, but more words won't do that, will they.
This is normally where I'd find a distraction, except I don't want the person we lost to become something we talk past.
My ballot was a decision, not the end of every doubt I had, though I understand why those might look similar from outside.
I chose according to what I could assess, and I can describe that without pretending I received a perfect answer from somewhere.
There's a longer explanation for my vote, naturally, but it begins with taking responsibility for the choice instead of the volume around it.
I spent a lot of time considering what to do, then had to stop considering long enough to actually cast the ballot.
My vote reflects my judgement at the time, with all the uncertainty included rather than quietly edited out afterward.
I didn't choose because I ran out of words, although that would be a remarkable event worth investigating separately.
You can question my ballot, and I'll answer, but please ask one question before I start supplying twelve answers.
I meant the choice I made, even if my explanation has wandered through several other places on the way here.
I weighed what I had, made a decision, and now have approximately three times as much to say about having made it.
The short version is that I cast my own vote; the long version would probably carry us into tomorrow.
I'm defending {target}. I don't want that simple point buried in the amount I tend to say.
Please hear {target}'s defense. I'm supporting them, and giving them time seems a reasonable place to start.
I'm backing {target} for now. That doesn't mean I think we should stop asking sensible questions.
I don't support condemning {target}. Let them answer the accusation before we decide.
My support is with {target}. It's a judgement under uncertainty, but it is still my judgement.
I'm defending {target} rather than joining the accusation. I wanted to make that distinction clear.
I checked {target}, and before I explain how many times I rehearsed saying it, the result was {result}.
Here's the important finding, followed by no unnecessary introduction if I can help it: {target} appeared {result}.
My investigation returned {result} for {target}, which is what I need recorded rather than my whole account of preparing this announcement.
I've got a result to share, not a story, though habit makes them hard to separate: {target}, {result}.
Let me give the readout first so nobody has to wait through me finding my place: {target} came back {result}.
I'm asking for a trial for {target}, because a formal hearing seems a better place for questions than my increasingly long introduction.
Could we bring {target} to a hearing and actually give the defense room to happen, rather than all discussing the idea of it?
My request is to put {target} on trial, and I should stop there before this becomes a speech about speeches.
I'd like {target} questioned formally, which is a specific proposal despite the amount of language I seem to have wrapped around it.
Let's open a trial for {target}; I have other thoughts, but they're less useful than making the request clear.
I deny the accusation against me, and I want to turn the question toward {target}. I suspect them.
Let me be clear before I wander: I reject the charge against me, and I'm accusing {target}.
I don't accept the case against me. We should be questioning {target}, which is the other point I'm trying to make.
I'm defending myself, but I'm also raising a suspicion of {target}. Please don't lose that second part in my answer.
I deny it. I want us to examine {target} instead of treating me as the only possible suspect.
I have several things I could say, which is why I'm trying the unusual approach of keeping all of them to myself.
I'll listen for a turn, though I should warn you that I am already composing a response to the idea of listening.
Nothing to add, and yes, this sentence is technically an addition, but I intend it to be the last one for now.
I'm stopping here before the next thought brings its entire family along.
Somebody else should take the floor; I've had enough contact with it for one turn.
I keep talking because if I stop, I can hear how worried I am, which is probably not the reassuring explanation I intended.
Every possible outcome seems to invite another possible outcome, and by the time I've considered them I don't feel safe in any room.
I was going to distract us with something ordinary, but apparently being frightened follows me even into the ordinary things.
Can somebody tell me how they stop imagining what tonight could bring, preferably in enough detail to keep me occupied?
I'm concerned, then concerned about how much I'm talking about being concerned, which is a fairly exhausting loop to stand inside.
Now that the role is public, I want to revisit what we heard, and I promise that doesn't mean reciting every conversation from the beginning.
That reveal changes the context, which means some of our earlier remarks deserve another look rather than merely a louder repetition.
I need a moment to fit the revealed role around the discussion we already had, because the picture is rearranging itself quite noisily.
We should go back over the claims with this new fact, though perhaps someone with a better sense of brevity should lead us.
There is the role, then everything we thought before learning it, and now the slightly uncomfortable business of putting those two together.
I thought I'd have more to say at the end, which is ridiculous considering how much I've had to say at every other point.
Please remember the useful part of what I told you, even if finding it requires a little patience with everything around it.
I could keep talking to make this moment last longer, but I know that's not really how time works.
My last request is that you let each other finish, something I admittedly spent a lot of our time making difficult.
I don't have a neat closing line, just the hope that you keep listening when the room gets smaller.
I have the night account ready, and I'll get to it before the introduction grows legs. {result}
Here's what I need recorded, with the side commentary held back for once. {result}
About last night, which is the subject I'm actually going to stay on this time. {result}
Let me read the account before I start explaining my explanation of it. {result}
The relevant part begins now, so please ignore the unnecessarily long runway. {result}
That is awkward, because I am the {role}, and I was saving that announcement for a much less awkward moment.
Hang on, we cannot both be the {role}, unless someone changed the roster, which they did not, so I am challenging that.
I had a whole explanation ready, but you have forced the short version: I am the actual {role}.
Normally I would let you finish, honestly I would, but claiming my job is a fairly major interruption. I am the {role}.
You know when someone tells your story as if it happened to them? This is that. I am the {role}.
Before this gets repeated and everyone starts remembering it wrong, let me put the correction on record: I am the {role}.
Well, there goes my quiet plan, not that it was especially quiet. I am the {role}, so that claim cannot stand.
I was waiting for a sensible opening, and apparently the opening is someone else taking my job. The {role} is me.
